stops.name: Broad Street, Soho, the birth
stops.campa: William Blake is born over his father's hosier's shop at 28 Broad Street, Soho, third surviving child of James Blake and Catherine Hermitage Blake. The street is loud with tradesmen's cries and looms southward toward the fields that still edge London. He is christened at St James's, Piccadilly, a few days on. Nothing yet marks the house as different from its neighbors, but the boy who will see angels in these rooms and this small garden is already breathing London's coal-smoke air, and already, his family will later say, unlike other children from the first.

stops.name: Broad Street, God at the window
stops.campa: A small boy of four looks up and God puts His head to the window and screams, and the child screams too, in terror at the nearness of it. This is the first of the visions, told afterward by the family as the plain truth of what happened in that upstairs room, not a dream reported at breakfast but a visitation that frightened a small child badly enough to be remembered a lifetime. No one in the house on Broad Street has seen anything like it before or since. The boy does not forget the shape of that face at the glass.

stops.name: Peckham Rye, the tree filled with angels
stops.campa: Walking out to Peckham Rye, still open country south of the river, the boy of eight looks up into an oak and sees it filled with angels, their wings bespangling every bough like stars. He runs home and tells it plainly, as a thing seen. His father, a hard practical man, is ready to thrash him for lying; only his mother, Catherine, stands between them and saves him the beating. The vision is never retracted. Decades later Blake will still name Peckham Rye as the place where Heaven first opened over an English common.

stops.name: Henry Pars' Drawing School, the Strand
stops.campa: James Blake, seeing that his son's gift will not be argued out of him, spares the ordinary schooling and sends the boy of ten instead to Henry Pars' drawing school in the Strand, to copy from plaster casts of antique statuary. His father gives him small sums to buy prints at the auction houses, and the boy comes home with engravings after Raphael, Michelangelo, Dürer and Marten Heemskerck, poring over them instead of playmates. He is already forming the taste, half-Gothic and half-antique, that will set him against every fashionable painter of his century.

stops.name: Great Queen Street, apprenticed to James Basire
stops.campa: At fourteen, too old-fashioned in his tastes for the fashionable painter Blake's father first proposed, the boy is bound apprentice for seven years to James Basire, engraver to the Society of Antiquaries, at his shop in Great Queen Street. Here he learns the plain, hard, linear discipline of the burin, unlike the softer stipple then coming into vogue, a discipline he will call, all his life, the true and correct line against the blotting and blurring of the moderns. Basire is a sound and honest master. The trade Blake is given here will still be feeding him at his death.

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, the opened tomb of Edward I
stops.campa: Basire, wanting to separate his quarreling apprentices, sends young Blake alone into Westminster Abbey to draw the royal monuments for Richard Gough's Sepulchral Monuments. On the second of May the antiquaries open the tomb of Edward I, dead four hundred and fifty years, to examine the body within, and Blake is set to record it. He climbs among effigies of Henry III, Queen Eleanor, Queen Philippa, Edward III, Richard II, spending whole days alone in the vaulted quiet, the Gothic line entering his hand so deeply that it will outlast every fashion he is ever asked to imitate.

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, the vision of Christ and the Apostles
stops.campa: Alone in the long aisles among the tombs he is set to copy, the light falling through the clerestory, Blake sees the aisles filled: Christ walking among his twelve Apostles, a great procession of monks and priests behind them, and hears their chant rise into the vaulting as if the stones themselves were still singing the offices ended centuries before. It comes to him here as plainly as the Abbey's own carved stone, unbidden, while his pencil is still on the paper. He does not ask whether it is a granted grace or a common one; he only draws, after, more surely.

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, the quarrel with the Westminster schoolboys
stops.campa: The boys of Westminster School, let into the Abbey on old privilege, find the solitary apprentice on his scaffold an easy mark and taunt him at his drawing until one goes too far. Blake, no lover of being trifled with even as a boy, knocks him down from the scaffold to the pavement below. He goes at once to the Dean to lay his complaint rather than wait to be blamed, and the Dean, hearing him out, withdraws the schoolboys' privilege of the Abbey entirely. The vaulted aisles are quiet again, and Blake's solitary hours among the Gothic dead resume undisturbed.

stops.name: Old Somerset House, Royal Academy student
stops.campa: His apprenticeship out, Blake enters the Royal Academy schools at Old Somerset House as a student, free of fee but bound to find his own materials for six years. He falls in at once with John Flaxman, Thomas Stothard and George Cumberland, sharing their radical politics as freely as their studios, and comes to admire the fierce independence of Fuseli and James Barry over the polished manner Sir Joshua Reynolds, the Academy's president, holds up as law. Blake sets Michelangelo and Raphael's hard clean line against Reynolds's oil-shadowed fashion, and never afterward troubles to hide his contempt for the Academy's taste.

stops.name: St Mary's Church, Battersea, the marriage
stops.campa: Nursing a heartbreak from a woman who refused him, Blake tells the whole sorry story to a gardener's daughter called Catherine Boucher and her family in Battersea. When he asks her, 'Do you pity me?' and she answers that she does, he declares on the spot, 'Then I love you,' and within the year marries her at St Mary's, Battersea, on the eighteenth of August. Catherine, unable to read or write, signs the register with her mark. Blake will teach her to read, to draw, to color his plates and pull his prints, and she will outlive him only four years, faithful to the end.
stops.quote: Do you pity me? ... Then I love you.
stops.quote_source: Recounted in Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), of Blake's proposal to Catherine Boucher, 1781-82

stops.name: Broad Street, Poetical Sketches printed
stops.campa: Friends of the household, chiefly the Reverend Anthony Stephen Mathew and the sculptor Flaxman, put up the money to have Blake's early verses set in ordinary type and printed as Poetical Sketches, the only book of his ever produced by a conventional press rather than his own hand. The poems, some written as young as twelve, already carry the plain, singing, half-archaic diction that will run through everything he writes after. He will never again trust a printer with his words; from here the page itself becomes something he must make, not merely fill.

stops.name: Broad Street, the print shop and the father's death
stops.campa: James Blake dies in July, and William, with his old schoolfellow James Parker, opens a print-selling shop next door to the family home at 27 Broad Street, taking his younger brother Robert in as an assistant and pupil. Robert, gentle and gifted, has followed William's own hand and eye almost from birth, and the two work the counter and the graver together. It is a hard trade in a hard year, but the brothers are close in a way William will not be close to any other living soul, and the shop keeps them under one roof daily.
